summary: Contains definitions of managed objects used as experimental extensions to the generic interfaces structure of MIB-II. It was on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 1573.

plainLanguage.summary: Network management works by giving devices a set of named values to report, such as a count of packets sent. This RFC adds a few more values for network interfaces: what hardware is in them, a way to ask an interface to test itself, and a list of the addresses each interface will accept.

subtitle: Extra managed objects for the standard network interface table: hardware details, interface tests and accepted addresses.

tldr.problem: The standard interface table in MIB-II covers only what is common to every network interface, so information specific to an interface had no agreed place to go.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three new tables under one experimental branch of the management tree: an extension table with per-interface facts, a test table that lets a manager run an interface test, and a table listing the addresses an interface will accept.
tldr.outcome: The module was defined as an experimental extension to MIB-II. This RFC was later obsoleted by RFC 1573.

sections.title: The Network Management Framework
sections.content:
The Internet-standard Network Management Framework consists of three components. RFC 1155 defines the SMI, the mechanisms used for describing and naming objects for the purpose of management, and RFC 1212 defines a more concise description mechanism that is wholly consistent with the SMI. RFC 1156 defines MIB-I, the core set of managed objects for the Internet suite of protocols, and RFC 1213 defines MIB-II, an evolution of MIB-I based on implementation experience and new operational requirements. RFC 1157 defines SNMP, the protocol used for network access to managed objects.

Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store, the Management Information Base. Objects in the MIB are defined using the subset of ASN.1 defined in the SMI. Each object has a name, a syntax and an encoding. The name is an object identifier, an administratively assigned name that specifies an object type; the object type together with an object instance serves to uniquely identify a specific instantiation of the object. For human convenience, a textual string, the OBJECT DESCRIPTOR, is also often used to refer to the object type. The syntax defines the abstract data structure, and the encoding is how that structure is represented on the network, using the basic encoding rules of ASN.1.
sections.plainLanguage: Network management works by defining named values that a device reports, such as a counter of packets sent. Each value has a dotted number as its name, which is how the tree of managed objects is numbered, and a readable name beside it for people.

sections.title: The Three Extension Tables
sections.content:
The Internet Standard MIB contains a group of management objects pertaining to a network device's generic network interfaces. These objects are generic in the sense that they apply to all network interfaces, irrespective of the type of communication media and protocols used on them. This has proved necessary but not sufficient: efforts are underway to define additional MIB objects which are specific to particular media and lower-level protocol stacks. Some of those efforts have identified objects which are required, or at least useful, but are not specific to the interface type the effort is focusing on, so it is better to define them as extensions to the generic interface group than to define them in multiple interface-type MIBs.

This memo defines the resulting extensions, spread over three tables: the generic Interface Extension table, the generic Interface Test table and the generic Receive Address table. The whole module is rooted at ifExtensions, whose object identifier is { experimental 6 }, so these objects live in the experimental subtree of the SMI. The first table is mandatory for all types of subnetwork interface, the test table is optional but must be implemented in full if the table is implemented, and the receive address table is mandatory for all interfaces that can receive packets or frames addressed to more than one address.
sections.plainLanguage: The extension objects are split into three tables. One holds general facts about an interface, one is for asking an interface to run a test, and one lists the addresses the interface will accept. All of them sit under one experimental branch of the management tree.

sections.title: The Generic Interface Test Table
sections.content:
The second table defines objects that allow a network manager to instruct an agent to test an interface for various faults. A few common types of test are defined in this document, but most will be defined elsewhere, dependent on the particular type of interface. After testing, the object ifExtnsTestResult can be read to determine the outcome, and ifExtnsTestCode provides further test-specific or interface-specific information about it. If an agent cannot perform the test, ifExtnsTestResult is set to say so.

Only one test can be in progress on each interface at any one time. If one test is in progress when another is invoked, the second test is rejected, and some agents may reject a test when a prior test is active on another interface. When a test is invoked, the agent saves the identity of the originator and the request-id in ifExtnsTestRequestId and ifExtnsTestCommunity, and those values remain set until the next test is invoked.

The test is started by writing an object identifier to the read-write object ifExtnsTestType. Writing the special value noTest takes no action unless a test is in progress, in which case the test is aborted; writing any other value is only valid when no test is currently in progress. This document assigns a value for a full-duplex loopback test. The result of the most recently requested test is one of none(1), success(2), inProgress(3), notSupported(4), unAbleToRun(5), aborted(6) or failed(7), and the detail code has a special value for use when no additional result code is available.
sections.plainLanguage: A manager asks an interface to test itself by writing a code into one entry. The agent reports back with a result and a detail code. Only one test can run on an interface at a time, so a second request is refused.

sections.title: The Generic Receive Address Table
sections.content:
The third table contains objects relating to an interface's support for receiving packets or frames at more than one address on the same interface. It has an entry for each address, broadcast, multicast or unicast, for which the system will receive packets or frames on a particular interface. When an interface is operating in promiscuous mode, entries are only required for those addresses for which the system would receive frames were it not operating in that mode.

Each entry holds the ifIndex of the interface that recognises the address, the address itself as a physical address, and a status object with four values: other(1) for entries that are valid and exist but are not classified as to whether they will continue to exist after the next restart, invalid(2) for entries that do not represent an address the interface accepts, volatile(3) for entries that are valid and exist but have not been saved, and nonVolatile(4) for entries that are valid and will not be deleted by the next restart of the managed system. The default for a new entry is volatile. Management stations must be prepared to receive tabular information corresponding to entries that are not currently in use, and must examine the status object to interpret them properly.
sections.plainLanguage: This table lists every address an interface will accept, and says whether each one is kept across a restart of the managed system or only exists until the next one.

sections.title: The Generic Interface Extension Table
sections.content:
The first table consists of new objects applicable to all types of subnetwork interface, and the group is mandatory for all of them. It holds one entry per interface, indexed by the same ifIndex value used by the standard interface table, so an entry can be matched to the interface it describes.

The objects in an entry are ifExtnsIfIndex, an integer identifying the interface; ifExtnsChipSet, an object identifier naming the hardware chip set, with the identifier unknownChipSet returned when the chip set is unknown; ifExtnsRevWare, a display string of up to 255 characters describing the firmware version, which is intended to be human readable; four counters for multicast and broadcast frames successfully transmitted and received; and ifExtnsPromiscuous, an integer with the value true(1) when the station accepts all packets or frames transmitted on the media, and false(2) when it accepts only those addressed to this station. The value true(1) is only legal on certain types of media, and setting it may require the interface to be reset before it takes effect.
sections.plainLanguage: For each interface this table records the chip set and firmware version, four counters for multicast and broadcast traffic, and whether the interface accepts all traffic on the wire or only what is addressed to it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section of the memo says that security issues are not discussed in it. The memo is a set of managed object definitions and the rules for using them, and the access of each object, such as which are read-only and which are read-write, is the only thing it says about who may change what.

The definitions are also experimental. The memo states that the framework permits new objects to be defined for the purpose of experimentation and evaluation, and the module as a whole sits under the experimental branch of the SMI rather than in a standards-track branch.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo says nothing about security. It only defines the objects and says which of them a manager may read and which it may change.
